name: Knee Osteoarthritis
summary: Knee osteoarthritis (knee OA) is a long-term joint condition in which the whole knee is affected: cartilage, bone, the joint lining, ligaments and the muscles around it. It is one of the most common causes of pain and walking difficulty in adults.

looksLike: Knee pain that builds with activity such as walking, stairs, kneeling and rising from a chair, and eases with rest.
Short morning stiffness (usually under about 30 minutes) or stiffness after sitting.
Grating or creaking (crepitus), swelling from time to time, bony enlargement, reduced bend or straightening.
A feeling of the knee giving way from thigh muscle weakness or pain.
Usually age 45 or older, or after a past injury such as ACL or meniscal injury, or with overweight.
redFlags: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or unable to move the joint
Sudden hot swollen painful joint, no fever
Injury with inability to take weight, bony tenderness, or inability to bend to 90 degrees, age 55 or older

Priority: build strength, fitness and confidence.

assess: Observe alignment (bow-legged or knock-kneed), swelling, muscle wasting and gait.

blocks.text: **Knee osteoarthritis (knee OA)** is a long-term joint condition in which the whole knee is affected: cartilage, bone, the joint lining, ligaments and the muscles around it. It is one of the most common causes of pain and walking difficulty in adults [Ref - to verify]. It most often affects the inner (medial) compartment and the patellofemoral joint.

The common description of OA as simple wear and tear is not accurate. Joint changes on X-ray do not always match pain or function. Many people with X-ray changes have little pain, and some people with severe pain have mild X-ray changes [Ref - to verify]. Treatment therefore focuses on symptoms, function and participation.

items: Knee pain that builds with activity such as walking, stairs, kneeling and rising from a chair, and eases with rest.
Short morning stiffness (usually under about 30 minutes) or stiffness after sitting.
Grating or creaking (crepitus), swelling from time to time, bony enlargement, reduced bend or straightening.
A feeling of the knee giving way from thigh muscle weakness or pain.
Usually age 45 or older, or after a past injury such as ACL or meniscal injury, or with overweight [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: In many guidelines, knee OA can be diagnosed clinically in a person aged 45 or older with activity-related knee pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting under 30 minutes, without routine imaging [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: Honest note: no special test confirms knee OA. Findings of age, pain pattern, crepitus, bony enlargement and limited movement together support a clinical diagnosis. Function and strength measures are used to guide and monitor treatment.
E1. Effusion tests

rows: Supine, knee extended; stroke fluid up the inner side of the knee, then stroke down the outer side
A bulge appears on the inner side
Supine, knee extended; push fluid out of the suprapatellar pouch with one hand, tap the patella down with the other hand
The patella floats and taps against the femur

blocks.text: A warm, tense effusion with fever or severe pain is a red flag (see G).
E2. Range and crepitus

Measure knee flexion and extension with a goniometer where possible. Record loss of full extension. Palpate during movement for crepitus. Loss of movement with a hard end-feel suggests structural change.
E3. Functional performance tests (core set)

Commonly recommended simple tests include the 30-second chair stand, the timed up and go (TUG) and a fast-paced walk test over a measured distance, with stair climb as an option [Ref - to verify]. Record baseline values, and repeat to track progress. Do not quote norm values until sources are verified.
E4. Patient-reported measures
Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), WOMAC or the Oxford Knee Score, and a 0 to 10 pain scale [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Hot, red, swollen knee with fever or unable to move the joint
Same-day hospital; do not exercise or mobilise
Sudden hot swollen painful joint, no fever
Injury with inability to take weight, bony tenderness, or inability to bend to 90 degrees, age 55 or older
Use local injury decision rule (such as the Ottawa knee rules) and refer for imaging [Ref - to verify]
Calf swelling, warmth, pain, or sudden breathlessness

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Age 45 or over, activity-related knee pain, short or no morning stiffness? **Yes:** working diagnosis is knee OA (routine imaging is not needed).
Findings suggest another cause (locking, long morning stiffness, injury, hip pain)? Use that pathway.
Start core treatments: education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
If symptoms remain severe and function is poor despite good non-surgical care, discuss specialist review for injections or joint replacement [Ref - to verify].

rows: May give short-term pain relief and movement gains [Ref - to verify]
Supine or sitting, gentle tibiofemoral and patellar glides, low to moderate grade

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and exercise. Manual therapy is optional as a short-term adjunct, usually combined with exercise. Do not claim that it restores cartilage or reverses the arthritis. Evidence for manual therapy alone is low in certainty [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** exercise is a first-line treatment for knee OA in nearly all major guidelines [Ref - to verify]. A common approach combines strengthening with aerobic activity, two to three times a week, supervised or as a home program. The type of exercise matters less than doing it regularly, progressing it gradually and continuing it.

rows: Stand up from a chair and sit slowly
Pain above about 4 out of 10 that lasts into the next day
Straight leg raise or seated knee extension
Lift the leg with a light weight if needed
Use a rail, step up and control the step down
Lying on the side, lift the top leg
10 to 20 minutes, 3 to 5 days a week
Range exercise (heel slides, knee extension holds)

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain during exercise up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within about 24 hours is generally acceptable [Ref - to verify]. Pain that rises sharply, a hot swollen knee, or new instability means reduce load and reassess.

**Weight management:** if the patient is overweight, even modest weight loss can reduce pain [Ref - to verify]. Discuss respectfully, using the patient's goals, and refer to a dietitian when available.

**Aids:** a walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful knee may reduce load. Supportive, cushioned footwear is advised. Routine use of lateral wedge insoles is not recommended in several guidelines [Ref - to verify]. Knee braces may help selected patients.

rows: Short-term comfort before or after exercise
Short-term pain relief; limited long-term benefit [Ref - to verify]
May reduce pain in some patients; limited evidence

blocks.text: **Medical options (decided by doctors):** topical anti-inflammatory gels, oral medication, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief of flares, and total or partial knee replacement for severe cases [Ref - to verify]. Rehabilitation before and after surgery improves readiness and recovery, and follows the surgeon's protocol.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 63-year-old teacher has 18 months of bilateral knee pain, worse on stairs and after walking, with 15 minutes of morning stiffness. Her right knee has crepitus, mild effusion and reduced flexion. She is overweight and avoids walking. Hip examination is normal. No fever, no calf swelling, no injury.

**Working diagnosis:** bilateral knee osteoarthritis. **Plan:** education, a regular strengthening and walking program, weight support, a stick on the left in the right hand, footwear review, measure chair stand and TUG, reassess every 4 to 6 weeks.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is X-ray not required for diagnosis here? The age, pain pattern and short stiffness are enough for a clinical diagnosis in most guidelines, and X-ray findings do not always match symptoms [Ref - to verify].
Why is exercise a core treatment even when the knee hurts? It improves pain, strength and function in many people, and avoiding movement tends to worsen weakness and stiffness [Ref - to verify].
The knee suddenly becomes hot and swollen and the patient has a fever. What do you do? Stop, refer to hospital the same day for possible joint infection.
Why not promise that the knee will be cured? OA is long-term, but symptoms can improve and be controlled with regular activity and self-management.
Why test chair stand and TUG? They measure real-life function and provide a baseline to track progress.
**Initial approach:** education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
**Justifying findings:** age, activity-related pain, short stiffness, crepitus, no flags.
**Priority:** build strength, fitness and confidence.
**Manual therapy:** optional short-term adjunct.
**Exercise:** strengthening plus aerobic work, 2 to 3 times a week.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** OA is manageable, movement helps, flares are normal.
**Avoid:** prolonged rest, promises of cure, routine reliance on ultrasound.
**Measure:** pain, KOOS or WOMAC, chair stand, TUG.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** self-management plan and maintenance exercise in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no infection, no fracture, no inflammatory arthritis.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise, weight loss and education improve pain and function; how different exercise types compare.
**Hypotheses:** that strength training protects joints (uncertain); that mobilization works via pain modulation.
**Future questions:** best exercise dose, and which patients benefit from surgery earlier.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

Measure effusion, range and function.
